guide.title: Haydn, String Quartet Op. 64 No. 5 – II. Adagio cantabile: Listening Guide
guide.overview: This is a slow, songlike movement in 3/4 time. Its home key is A major. The first violin mostly sings the tune while the other three players accompany. The main tune comes back several times, and the music keeps returning to A major after short trips to other keys. Keys and chords here are estimated by computer, so they may be imperfect.

listening_points.headline: The main tune opens softly in Violin 1
listening_points.text: Violin 1 plays the main theme at the start, softly [m. 1-2]. The other parts accompany. The movement begins in A major, which is the home key.

listening_points.headline: Sharp accents colour the soft tune
listening_points.text: Several short, sharp accents (marked sf) appear in [m. 3-6]. They stand out against the soft playing. The music stays in A major and stays soft.

listening_points.headline: The main tune repeats
listening_points.text: The opening tune returns in Violin 1 at the same pitch [m. 9-10]. Listen for the familiar shape of the first notes.

listening_points.headline: A move to E major
listening_points.text: The key estimate moves to E major [m. 12-18]. This is a modulation, a change of key, so the tune sounds as if it has moved to a new place. Violin 1 leads and the others accompany.

listening_points.headline: A darker turn to A minor
listening_points.text: The key turns to A minor [m. 19-22], which gives a darker colour. In [m. 19] the parts move together in a chordal texture. Then the tune returns to the top line.

listening_points.headline: The main tune comes back in A major
listening_points.text: The opening tune returns in Violin 1 at the original pitch [m. 23-24]. It feels like a homecoming after the minor-key passage.

listening_points.headline: A short visit to D major
listening_points.text: The key moves to D major for a few bars [m. 26-29]. By [m. 29] the music drops to very soft (pp) and the parts move together.

listening_points.headline: A sudden loud peak, then calm
listening_points.text: The music jumps to loud (f) at [m. 31]. A computer estimate marks this as the loudest and busiest point. The parts play independent lines there. Loud playing continues to [m. 33], then the music is soft again at [m. 34].

listening_points.headline: A new section begins in A minor
listening_points.text: A new section starts with a new key signature [m. 35]. The key is A minor and the music stays soft. The lead at [m. 35] is uncertain, but probably Violin 2. Violin 1 then takes the tune [m. 36].

listening_points.headline: A lighter spell in C major
listening_points.text: The key brightens to C major [m. 40-46]. Violin 1 mostly leads with the others accompanying in [m. 41-45]. At [m. 40] and [m. 46] the lines are more independent.

listening_points.headline: Back toward A major with a swell
listening_points.text: The key goes briefly to A minor [m. 47-48], then to A major [m. 49]. A crescendo marking appears at [m. 50]. A crescendo means getting gradually louder.

listening_points.headline: The last section opens in A major
listening_points.text: The third section starts with a new key signature [m. 51]. It begins in A major, the home key, with Violin 1 leading. The other parts accompany, and sharp accents return in [m. 53-56].

listening_points.headline: The earlier key trips return
listening_points.text: The music goes to E major [m. 62-67], then to A minor [m. 68-72]. This is the same key path as before in [m. 12-22]. Violin 1 leads and the others accompany.

listening_points.headline: Home key, then D major, then very soft
listening_points.text: The music returns to A major [m. 73-75] and then visits D major [m. 76-79]. It gets very soft (pp) at [m. 79]. This repeats the key pattern from the first part.

listening_points.headline: A quiet fade in A major
listening_points.text: The ending stays in A major and very soft (pp) [m. 80-82]. A diminuendo marking appears at [m. 83]. A diminuendo means getting gradually softer. The last bar is soft (p) with the parts moving together.

glossary.explanation: The home note and scale that a passage seems to be built around. A change of key can brighten or darken the mood.
A move from one key to another.
One part sings the tune while the others play a supporting background.
The parts move together in the same rhythm, like a hymn.
Each part follows its own path, with no single clear tune.
A sudden, sharp accent on a note.
Gradually getting louder, or gradually getting softer.

review.note: prose corrected after a line-by-line review against the facts
